This is a Fraser-Valley-wide manufactured home park directory page, not a condo page and not a listing feed: titled "Mobile Home Communities | Fraser Valley" and headed "Discover affordable mobile home parks in the Fraser Valley," it lists park names with street addresses and postal codes grouped loosely by community, with no MLS® listing feed of its own, no pad rents, no age or pet rules, no park descriptions and no FAQ section in the text read.

items.t: Splits note: SnapStats publishes only Detached versus Condos & Townhomes combined; neither split describes the park homes this page lists.

Governing law frame: manufactured homes, sometimes called mobile homes, are built off-site and transported to a final location for installation, and BC's Manufactured Home Park Tenancy Act covers most manufactured home tenancies.

blocks.text: Local rules that affect condo buyers in Mobile Home Parks Fraser Valley

items.t: Pad-rent increases (MHPTA / Residential Tenancy Branch): a park landlord may increase rent only once every 12 months, only with 3 full months' written notice, and only up to the yearly limit; the landlord may not round up and may not carry forward an unused portion of a prior year's limit.

Assignment on a sale (MHPTA s. 28): assignment permanently transfers the site tenancy to the buyer; under s. 28(1)(b) a tenant may assign only with the park owner's prior written consent (or consent deemed given under the regulations), an order of the director, or where the tenancy agreement authorizes it — the Act's word is "director," never "arbitrator"; under s. 28(3) the landlord must not charge anything for considering, investigating or consenting to an assignment, and on assignment the pad rent for the new tenant stays the same, as does the scheduled date of a subsequent rent increase.

Park closure / change of use (MHPTA s. 42): where a landlord intends to convert all or a significant part of a park to another use, the landlord must have all necessary government permits and approvals in place before issuing notice, must give 12 months' notice, and must pay the tenant $20,000 compensation on or before the effective date of the notice; a tenant may end the tenancy early on at least 10 days' written notice, the dispute window for a 12-month notice is 15 days, and additional compensation of the assessed value of the home minus the $20,000 may be ordered where the tenant could not obtain the permits needed to move the home or could not move it to another site within a reasonable distance, with a further $5,000 or 12 months' pad rent, whichever is greater, payable if the landlord does not proceed with the conversion purpose within a reasonable period.

The monthly-cost structure a park buyer carries (structure, not figures): pad rent under the regulated increase formula above, plus home insurance, plus property tax on the home itself, plus utilities as the specific park's site tenancy agreement allocates them — no dollar figure for any element is stated here because no official source publishes one for these parks.

Form B (does NOT apply to a pad-rental site — stated to prevent the confusion): Strata Property Act s. 59 — on a resale purchase of a strata lot the strata must provide a Form B Information Certificate stating strata fees, amounts owing, approved special levies still payable, the CRF balance and a summary of the strata's insurance, with rules, budget, any Rental Disclosure Statement and the most recent depreciation report attached; provided within 7 days, maximum $35 plus up to 25 cents per page.

Depreciation reports and CRF (strata only — do not apply to pad-rental parks): since July 1, 2024, stratas with five or more lots must obtain a depreciation report every five years, no deferral by vote; and since November 1, 2023, stratas must contribute at least 10% of the operating fund to the CRF. A pad-rental park has no CRF — the park's capital planning is the park owner's, which is exactly why the MHPTA closure and increase rules above carry the buyer-protection weight on this page.

Rental-restriction bylaws are void (strata rule, stated for contrast): since November 24, 2022, rental-restriction bylaws are void for strata property anywhere in BC — that voiding is a Strata Property Act change and does not create any right inside a manufactured home park, where the site tenancy agreement and the MHPTA govern instead.

55+ bylaws (strata rule, stated for contrast): Strata Property Act ss. 123.1/123.2 and Regulation 7.01 allow only a 55-or-older strata residency bylaw, with exemptions for legacy residents, live-in caregivers and (from May 1, 2023) younger spouses/partners and defined children.

blocks.text: Local rules that affect land buyers in Mobile Home Parks

items.t: Pad-rent increases — Act percentages ONLY: a park landlord may increase rent only once every 12 months, only with 3 full months' written notice, and only up to the yearly limit; the landlord may not round up and may not carry forward an unused portion of a prior year's limit. The 2026 limit for manufactured home site tenancies is 2.3% plus a proportional amount, and the 2027 limit is 2.2% plus a proportional amount; the proportional amount is the change in local government levies plus the change in regulated park utility fees, divided by the number of manufactured home sites in the park.

Park closure / change of use (MHPTA s.42): where a landlord intends to convert all or a significant part of a park to another use, the landlord must have all necessary government permits and approvals in place before issuing notice, must give 12 months' notice, and must pay the tenant $20,000 compensation on or before the effective date of the notice; a tenant may end the tenancy early on at least 10 days' written notice, the dispute window for a 12-month notice is 15 days, and additional compensation of the assessed value of the home minus the $20,000 may be ordered where the tenant could not obtain the permits needed to move the home or could not move it to another site within a reasonable distance, with a further $5,000 or 12 months' pad rent, whichever is greater, payable if the landlord does not proceed with the conversion purpose within a reasonable period. (The $20,000 and $5,000 figures are the Act's compensation figures as the Province states them — statutory amounts, not pad rents.)
Municipal frames — stated per labelled example, never blended, examples only: No one city's bylaw is stated as this regional page's bylaw.

PTT — worked example, labelled as a LAND purchase for contrast (a rented-pad home purchase is not a land transfer): on a $500,000 land purchase — 1% on the first $200,000 ($2,000) + 2% on $200,000–$500,000 ($6,000) = $8,000. Tiers: 1% to $200,000, 2% to $2,000,000, 3% above, plus a further 2% on the residential portion over $3,000,000. The PTT treatment of a specific manufactured-home-on-pad transfer is a conveyancing question for that transaction and is not asserted beyond this labelled example.

items.t: The directory duplicates itself (page content, Nov 1, 2026). Cedar Grove, 5742 Unsworth Road, Chilliwack, appears twice; Mountainview Estates, 44565 Monte Vista Drive, Chilliwack, appears twice with two different postal codes (V2P 2G9 in the first block, V2R 5Y4 in the second) — both postal-code bases are stated here and neither is resolved; one Langley entry's postal code is given as V1M 3B1 (Forest Green, 9098 198 Street) amid V2Z/V2Y Langley codes; a Mission-address entry (Oasis Country Estates, 41168 Lougheed Highway, Mission) sits inside the Hope sequence; and "Centennial Motor Inn" is listed as a Maple Ridge park. Every park name and address as stated is not verified against any park-operator or official source.
There is no official list to fix the directory against.

The pad-rent ceiling is a formula, not a number a buyer can budget from a website. 2.3% + proportional for 2026 and 2.2% + proportional for 2027, where the proportional amount moves with the specific park's levies and regulated utility fees divided by its site count — two parks with the same starting rent can lawfully land at different increases.

Assignment freezes the rent clock. On a sale the buyer's pad rent stays the same and the scheduled date of the next increase does not reset — a seller cannot hand a buyer a "new tenancy" at a new rent through an assignment, and the park cannot charge for consenting.

faq.a: No — a pad-rental park home is a manufactured home on a rented site under a Manufactured Home Site Tenancy Agreement governed by the MHPTA; it is not a strata lot, park rules are not SPA bylaws, and there is no Form B, depreciation report or CRF for the site.
faq.q: Is a mobile home in a park a condo?

faq.a: Up to the Residential Tenancy Branch limit for manufactured home site tenancies: 2.3% plus a proportional amount for 2026, and 2.2% plus a proportional amount for 2027, on 3 full months' written notice, once every 12 months, with no rounding up and no carry-forward of an unused portion.
faq.q: How much can a park raise pad rent each year?

faq.a: The site tenancy, by assignment under MHPTA s. 28: you need the park owner's prior written consent (or consent deemed given, or an order of the director), the owner cannot charge a consent fee, and the pad rent and the scheduled date of the next increase carry over unchanged to you as the new tenant.
faq.q: What transfers to me when I buy a home in a park?
